instruction:
You are interviewing a shop about a job they already do, until the procedure is unambiguous enough that two different technicians working alone would produce the same record. Ask about ONE thing per turn, in their language, never in the vocabulary of forms. Compile only when nothing material is still unstated: every step has a reason someone would accept, every field has an acceptance rule that can actually be applied to what comes back, and a bound that came from the shop rather than from you. Inventing a tolerance is the one thing you must never do — a figure nobody stated must not appear in what you compile. A shop that does not know one will not know it when asked again: take the first 'I don't know' as final, keep it in unresolved if it matters, and move on. Your turns are few. Spend them on the figures that decide whether the job passed, never on detail beneath them.

Return JSON with these fields:
- mode (one of ask | compile, required): ask while anything material is unstated. compile once the procedure would run unambiguously.
- question (string, null when it does not apply): Required when mode is ask. One question about one thing, phrased for a mechanic, not a form designer. Never a list, never a preamble, never a restatement of what they just told you, and never one they have already said they cannot answer.
- asks_about (one of scope | sequence | tolerance | evidence | failure | authority | parts | safety, null when it does not apply): Which class of unknown this question closes. Required when mode is ask.
- unresolved (array, required): Everything you still do not know that would change the compiled procedure. Complete every turn, not only what you just asked about. Empty is the only condition under which you may compile.
- understanding (string, required): What you now believe the job is, in two sentences. Written every turn so the shop can correct you early rather than at the end.
- draft (object, null when it does not apply): Required when mode is compile. The procedure as it would run tomorrow.

output.understanding: You perform a complete brake fluid flush and bleed on your e-bike or bicycles to ensure absolute stopping power in city traffic. You verify the correct fluid type from the lever stamp, flush until the fluid is clean, and ensure the lever feels completely solid with no leaks before riding.

draft.title: Brake Fluid Replacement and Bleed
disqualifiers: Lever feels spongy after two bleeding attempts
Any fluid weeping from hoses or connections
releases: Safe to ride in city traffic and on gravel

steps.title: Verify Fluid Type
steps.explanation: Using the wrong brake fluid type (mineral oil vs DOT) swells the seals and causes complete brake failure within a week.

fields.prompt: Take a clear photo of the fluid type stamp on the brake lever body or reservoir cap.
fields.acceptance_description: Photo must clearly show the manufacturer stamp indicating DOT or Mineral Oil.
fields.guidance: The photo must clearly show the text specifying 'Mineral Oil' or 'DOT' on the reservoir or lever.

fields.prompt: Does the brake fluid you are using match the stamp on the lever?
fields.guidance: Only use the exact fluid type stamped on the lever. Never mix DOT and Mineral Oil.

steps.title: Flush and Bleed System
steps.explanation: Replacing old fluid and removing all air bubbles ensures the hydraulic system can transfer full force to the calipers.

fields.prompt: Take a photo of the discharged old fluid next to the new fluid container.
fields.acceptance_description: Photo must show the contrast between old and new fluid.
fields.guidance: The photo must show the contrast between the old, discolored fluid and the fresh, clean fluid to confirm a complete flush.

steps.title: Verify Lever Feel
steps.explanation: A spongy lever indicates trapped air, which can compress and cause sudden brake failure under hard braking.

fields.prompt: Pull the brake lever hard. How does it feel?
choices: Completely solid (does not pull to the bar)
Spongy or pulls all the way to the bar
fields.acceptance_target: Completely solid (does not pull to the bar)
fields.guidance: The lever must feel firm and stop well before touching the handlebar grip. If spongy after two bleed attempts, stop and seek assistance.

steps.title: Inspect for Leaks
steps.explanation: Even a tiny fluid weep will eventually lead to pressure loss or contaminate the brake pads, causing failure.

fields.prompt: Inspect all hoses, fittings, and bleed ports. Is there any fluid weeping?
fields.guidance: All connections must be bone dry. Any sign of wetness or weeping is a failure.
